summary: An April 1st joke memo defining a Management Information Base for drip-type heated beverage hardware, with objects for managing coffee-brewing and maintenance devices. It is humorous and was not meant to be implemented.

plainLanguage.summary: A pretend list of dials and gauges for checking on a coffee machine from far away. It is a joke.

questions: what is the coffee pot mib
subtitle: An April 1st joke: SNMP objects for monitoring a drip coffee pot, complete with pot type, level and temperature.

tldr.problem: Network management has a MIB for nearly everything, and this joke asks what it would take to manage a coffee machine in the same way.
tldr.mechanism: It defines a COFFEE-POT-MIB module with objects for the pot's name, capacity, brew type, location, operating status, level, start time and temperature.
tldr.outcome: It is an April 1st joke document, dated 1 April 1998. Its acknowledgements even credit a Networked Appliance Management Working Group with the words "(not) of the IETF".

today: RFC 2325 is an Informational April 1st joke, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text claims no real deployments.

sections.title: A Management Standard for Coffee
sections.content: RFC 2325 is an April 1st joke document, dated 1 April 1998. It plays the straight man: a deadpan extension to the Management Information Base (MIB) for network management, defining objects for coffee-brewing and maintenance devices. It leans on the real SMIv2 machinery, citing the SNMPv2 framework documents RFC 1442, RFC 1213, RFC 1445 and RFC 1448.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke is that it uses very serious network rules to talk about something as silly as a coffee pot.

sections.title: Scope and the Interface MIB
sections.content:
The COFFEE POT MIB applies to managed devices that brew, store and deliver heated coffee beverages, and it is declared mandatory for all systems that have such a hardware port supporting services managed through some other MIB. Its objects cover physical connections, configuration, storage levels, availability and quality of service.

The memo places the module in the Interface MIB's layering, as the lowest interface sublayer, the physical layer, serving higher layers such as the Character MIB. It admits that it is unlikely a coffee port will ever be used as a network interface. It says the module is relevant for ifType value sip(31) and requires the conformance groups ifGeneralGroup and ifFixedLengthGroup.
sections.plainLanguage: The note says every machine with a coffee port has to follow it, and then admits nobody will really plug a coffee pot into a network.

sections.title: The Coffee Pot Objects
sections.content:
The module is registered under transmission 132. Its objects are:

  • potName, potCapacity, potType and potLocation: a vendor description, the units of beverage the device supports, the brew type and the physical location.
  • potOperStatus: read-only status. The text notes that current hardware prevents changing the pot state via SNMP.
  • potLevel and potMetric: how much coffee there is, and the unit it is measured in.
  • potStartTime: seconds since Jan 1 1970 to start the pot, used only when the status is waiting.
  • lastStartTime and potTemperature: time since brewing began, and the ambient temperature of the coffee in degrees Centigrade.

Brew types are automatic-drip, percolator, french-press and espresso. Level units run from espresso through demi-tasse, cup and mug up to bucket.
sections.plainLanguage: The gauges tell you the pot's name, how big it is, what kind it is, where it sits, whether it is brewing, how full it is, and how warm the coffee is. A bucket is the biggest size.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in this memo. Like the rest of the document, it is brief and in character.
sections.plainLanguage: Nobody wrote anything about keeping coffee pots safe from pranksters.

items.desc: Waiting; the only state in which potStartTime applies.
